PSI-26: BASS burned small samples of everyday spacecraft materials aboard the International Space Station. Crews lit cotton-fiberglass fabric, Nomex, Ultem, acrylic (PMMA) and wax candles inside a sealed glovebox. A small fan blew air over each sample at controlled speeds, toward or away from the flame. The team watched whether each flame kept burning, shrank or went out as the airflow changed. They also tested how well a nitrogen gas spray, like the extinguisher used on the station, put the flames out. The goal was to see how real materials burn in space compared with NASA's standard tests on Earth.
PSI-25: BASS-II followed up on BASS with more materials, shapes and air conditions aboard the space station. Crews burned acrylic (PMMA) sheets, rods and spheres, cotton-fiberglass fabric and other samples in a small wind tunnel. They changed two things: how fast air flowed over the sample, and how much oxygen was in the air, lowering it below normal by adding nitrogen. Cameras recorded how flames started, grew, spread and went out. The results help show the lowest oxygen and airflow at which materials can still burn in space. They also feed the computer models used to design spacecraft fire detection and suppression systems.
PSI-98: Saffire-I was the first large fire test in space, run inside an empty cargo spacecraft after it left the space station. Burning something this big on the station itself would be too dangerous. A sheet of cotton-fiberglass fabric about 94 cm long and 40 cm wide was lit while fans pulled air past it. Cameras and sensors tracked how fast the fire grew and spread across the sheet. The aim was to learn how quickly a fire the size of a real cabin fire grows in near-weightless conditions. The results were compared with NASA's standard material screening tests on Earth.
PSI-99: Saffire-II repeated the large-scale fire test inside an empty cargo spacecraft, this time with nine smaller samples. The samples included cotton-fiberglass fabric, silicone, flat and shaped acrylic (PMMA), and acrylic placed next to Nomex. Each sample was 5 cm by 29 cm and was lit one at a time in a duct with fans pulling air through. Some samples burned fully while others would not light or stopped burning. The test showed which common spacecraft materials can keep a flame going in space at normal oxygen levels. It also compared those results with NASA's standard tests on Earth.
PSI-100: Saffire-III ran another large fire test inside an empty cargo spacecraft after it left the space station. It used the same cotton-fiberglass fabric as Saffire-I, but with faster airflow (30 cm/s instead of 20 cm/s). Air flowed either in the same direction the flame spread or against it. Cameras, temperature sensors and heat sensors recorded the fire as it grew. The goal was to see how airflow speed and direction change how fast a large fire spreads in space. These results help set safer limits for materials used on spacecraft.
PSI-69: FLEX lit single drops of liquid fuel, heptane and methanol, aboard the space station. With almost no gravity, each drop burns as a near-perfect sphere, which makes the flame easy to study. Crews changed the pressure, the oxygen level and the amount of added gases such as carbon dioxide and helium. Cameras recorded how long each drop burned and whether its flame went out before the fuel was used up. The goal was to find the conditions where fuel flames can no longer survive. This helps judge how well gases like carbon dioxide can put out fires in space.
PSI-68: FLEX-2 extended the FLEX droplet tests to fuels and conditions closer to those inside real engines. It burned single drops of pure fuels and of two-fuel mixtures aboard the space station. Pressure was varied from half to three times normal air pressure, and oxygen from 10% to 40%. The team studied how the fuels mix inside a burning drop, how soot forms and when flames go out. It also looked at how nearby drops affect each other's flames. The data are used to test and improve computer models of fuel burning.
PSI-39: The Cool Flames Investigation studied an unusual kind of flame that burns at a much lower temperature than a normal fire. Crews burned single drops of jet-fuel-like liquids, such as n-dodecane and mixtures with similar fuels, aboard the space station. These cool flames are very hard to study on Earth because gravity disturbs them. The tests varied pressure, drop size and the amount of helium in the surrounding gas. The team recorded when the cool flames formed and when they went out. The results help explain how fuels ignite inside engines.
PSI-10: Flame Design studied flames made by gas fuels, ethylene and methane, flowing out of a small ball-shaped burner. In space these flames form round shells, which makes them simpler to measure than flames on Earth. The team changed the fuel flow, the gas mixture and the pressure. They measured flame temperature, size, color and how much soot each flame made. They also found the conditions at which the flames went out. The goal is to learn how to design flames that burn cleaner and produce less soot.
PSI-20: The Burning Rate Emulator used gas flames on flat porous burners to imitate how solid materials and liquids burn. By choosing the gas flow, the team could stand in for many different real materials without burning them. Tests ran in still air at the oxygen and pressure levels planned for future crewed spacecraft. These included normal Earth air and lower-pressure, oxygen-rich cabin air. The team measured how strongly each flame burned and when it went out. The results help predict which materials could burn under future spacecraft cabin conditions.
PSI-21: The Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame investigation studied small, steady gas flames surrounded by a gentle flow of air. The fuels were methane and ethylene, sometimes thinned with other gases. Without gravity, these flames are longer and slower, which makes them easier to measure in detail. The team measured flame shape, how far the flame lifted off the burner, temperature and soot. They also found the conditions where the flames went out. The data are used to test and improve computer models of flames and soot.
PSI-22: E-FIELD Flames studied how an electric field changes the shape and behavior of a gas flame. A high voltage was applied between the burner and a metal mesh above it. In space, the effect of the electric field can be seen clearly without gravity getting in the way. The team measured the small electric current the flame carries and how the flame reacted when the voltage changed. They also looked at soot and at flames close to going out. The results could lead to new ways to control flames using electricity.
PSI-23: s-Flame studied round flames made by feeding gas fuels through a small ball-shaped burner aboard the space station. It tested both clean-burning fuel mixtures and sooty ones. The team measured how the flame's temperature and makeup changed as it formed and settled. They also found the conditions at which the flames went out. These measurements were compared with detailed computer simulations. The goal was to check how well those simulations describe real flames.
PSI-159: CFI-G studied cool flames made from gas fuels such as propane, butane and pentane. Cool flames burn at much lower temperatures than normal fires and are hard to keep going on Earth. The tests used a ball-shaped burner aboard the space station with different fuels, gas mixtures, flow rates and pressures. Cameras and sensors recorded when cool flames formed and how they behaved. The results were compared with computer simulations. The goal is to better understand the chemistry behind how fuels ignite.
PSI-107: SPICE studied when small gas flames start to give off smoke. Fuels such as methane, ethylene, propane and propylene burned from tiny nozzles inside a flow of air aboard the space station. The team slowly raised the fuel flow until each flame began releasing soot, called the smoke point. They also changed the nozzle size and the air speed around the flame. Cameras recorded the flame lengths at each setting. The results show how likely different fuels are to make smoke in space.
PSI-106: SLICE studied what holds a small gas flame onto its burner and what makes it lift off. Fuels such as methane and ethylene, sometimes mixed with nitrogen, burned in a flow of air aboard the space station. The team changed the fuel speed and burner size to find when each flame lifted away from the burner. They also looked at how much soot the flames made. More than 4,000 high-resolution images were captured. The results help check computer models of how flames stay stable.
PSI-102: SAME measured the smoke given off when common spacecraft materials are overheated, not when they burn. Crews heated material samples aboard the space station until they released smoke. Instruments and collection probes measured the size of the smoke particles. Smoke particles in space can be a different size than on Earth, which matters for smoke detectors. The goal was to understand smoke in space so that fires can be detected early. One problem was that many collected samples were later found to be contaminated.
PSI-101: SAME-R repeated the SAME smoke test aboard the space station with improvements. It added new materials, including a fire-resistant foam, and heated samples to higher temperatures. It also tried heating samples with no airflow. A new instrument replaced one of the old smoke measuring devices. The aim, like SAME, was to measure the size of smoke particles from overheated materials in space. These measurements help design better smoke detectors for spacecraft.
PSI-47: DAFT checked whether a common dust and smoke counter would work properly in space. The counter normally relies on gravity to recycle a liquid inside it, so NASA modified it to work without gravity. On the space station, the team released a standard test dust and measured it with both the modified counter and a trusted second instrument. They compared the two readings to see whether the modified counter was accurate. This test supported the later SAME smoke experiments. It made sure future smoke and dust measurements in space could be trusted.
